item.title: July 11, 2026
item.description:
I wanted to go far, very far so I could give myself some life. That was the whole reason. People keep telling me that I have "dead-inside vibes" and if I want to kill myself and instead of brushing it off I tell them the truth, no I don't want to die, not yet, because if I think about it, I haven't lived yet. It gives me this small weird hope that I genuinely hate, because hope is embarrassing and it asks something of you, but it's there I will get rid of it soon.

So I went. My closest friend lives a thousand kilometres from me and I actually did it! I got myself there, which if you know me is not nothing. It was unbearably hot where she is, the kind of heat I have no tolerance for and I would prefer to die in Antarctica instead of this heat. It makes me slow and stupid. And I had a good time. I want to write that plainly because I don't say it often and I don't want to dress it up: I genuinely had a good time. There is something about dragging your body somewhere it does not want to go, sweating through a heat you can't stand, just to sit next to one person who actually knows you that is maybe the most alive I have felt in a while. And she gave me something before I left, a poem book of Forough Farrokhzad in uzbek and I still don't have the words for what that did to me and that is a strange thing to admit as someone whose whole job is finding words. I read it the entire way back. There is something in Forough that goes straight. I don't know how she knew that was the exact thing to put in my hands. No I actually know how she knows, it was attention. And as Simone Weil said attention, taken to its highest degree is the same thing as prayer. Maybe that is what closest means.

Also one thing I keep wanting to tell someone. I bought the ticket from avtoticket.uz. And while I was in there trying to download the ticket, I saw interesting stuff. And according to Claude, the whole thing was running in debug mode, in production and one wrong turn handed me a stack trace and sitting inside that stack trace was its entire configuration file. The database login, the app key, a token for their Telegram bot, the credentials for the service that sends the SMS codes to your phone. I actually have everything to just get my laptop and turn down everything but something really keeps me from doing that. And it might just be laziness (or fear of letting my mom down)

![Stack trace exposing environment variables in production](img/avtoticket-1.png)

![Configuration values including app key, database and SMS credentials](img/avtoticket-2.png)

![More of the leaked environment: JWT secret, Telegram key and database block](img/avtoticket-3.png)

Anyways, it's true then, the thing everyone says and I never believed. You have to let things go. Physically and mentally I am trying. The physical part is almost the easier one, you buy the ticket, you get on you go. The mental part is the one I keep failing at, the letting go of people and of versions of things that already ended but at least I am facing the right direction now, which is more than I could say a month ago. Now I am making time for the real stuff again. I have a new translation coming out soon, Poe again, but a shorter one this time. (Stay tuned.) I won't say which. It feels good to have something that is just mine, that no grade and no manager gets to touch that I do only because I love the sentences and want them to exist in Uzbek. That, apparently, is what living looks like for me. And doing some technical translations as well.

I am writing this from Safia near IT Park, by the window, watching everyone else's life go past. There is an Uzum courier out there in the full purple outfit, purple bag and all and he looks so stressed, checking his phone every second waiting for an order or a client. The phone is plugged into a powerbank so he can keep going without stopping. It's 4:25 now so he isn't stopping any time soon, dinner rush is coming and the orders will only pile up. Good spot for him at least, right by IT Park where the offices are full of men far too busy thinking about work to think about anything else, men for whom food is a side project they remember only when their stomach makes them. A couple walks by, both look Russian, both blonde, shorts and water bottles, the guy in a white backpack covered in little gen-z symbols, and they look light in a way I notice. A man around forty with his daughter, just walking, going nowhere in particular. And a Coca-Cola truck parked outside Korzinka, waiting to unload. I have to laugh at that truck a little because last week I wrote a whole thing about not being able to escape this machine, Coca-Cola in every corner shop and at every wedding, the whole system we're already soaked in, and here it is, twenty metres from me while I sit and drink something and watch. This year I actually wanted to do my research on Coca-Cola specifically. There were reports that even consumed within normal limits their products had some concerning health issues, something to do with refrigeration, cold chain problems and I got curious because I have honestly never seen a reefer truck here maybe they exist, I read it online and couldn't be sure. I decided it wasn't solid enough to build a capstone on, so I left it and wrote about Agile teams instead and guess what I got a terrible grade for it. And now here's the joke: this summer I was shortlisted for an internship by Coca Cola İçecek and the thing that connects me to that exact truck, is supply chain. Which I do not want to do. But it is so much better than the customer service job I'm in right now that if they call me for an interview I'll probably say yes. That's the part I keep circling. I wrote an essay about not wanting to feed the machine and I might go work inside its logistics, and I'll do it because it's the better compromise.

item.title: July 5, 2026
item.description:
Found out recently that Red Hat supports Israel. So I fallen in love with Fedora and I have been trying to learn it for almost a month now and things started to make sense. So Fedora is sponsored by RedHat and Red Hat is owned by IBM and it's not really a clean company as I consider. My first instinct was Fedora is open source, I don't pay for it, it's free and community version. So how could my using it profit them at all? It's a clean argument I would say but it's tied to Red Hat Enterprise Linux which is the one corporations pay money and Fedora is definitely a training ground. We are taught that value only means money, that if we are not swiping a card then we are not part of it, we are just watching from the side. But attention and data is value. Getting used to a brand is also value. Being one more body in the crowd that makes a thing look normal and permanent and inevitable is value. You can boycott with your wallet closed and still be feeding the machine with everything else you have. That's a genius approach actually but anyways.

And think about how normal all of it is. I live in Tashkent, there is a KFC that people gom there is Coca-Cola on every market, in every corner shop, at every wedding I have ever been to. Nobody reads the ownership chain before they drink. And I am not saying this from some clean height like I am better than any of them because I am not and I do drink that exact Coke and stand in KFC line. The brands are so deep in ordinary life that stepping out of them does not feel normal, isn't it insane? It feels like telling people I will no longer breathe a particular kind of air. That is the true win of a corporation, the one they do not even have to fight for anymore. You can't even picture a normal life wihtout it.

Also there's a part where complicates things, sometimes boycotting works. In March of 2024 the group that runs Starbucks across the Middle East, Alshaya, laid off more than two thousand people because the boycott had hollowed out their sales, branches closed. By 2025 Starbucks had posted three straight quarters of falling revenue and said it would shut dozens more stores. McDonalds had its first real sales miss in about four years and stock dropped by something close to seven billion dollars. In some Arab countries its sales fell somewhere between fifty and ninety percent in a single month. It got bad enough that McDonalds bought its entire Israeli franchise back it was 200+ restaurants if I'm not mistaken.

So why can't I just go and make tea instead of Coke? I got my own reasons: 2K+ people were fired in Amman and Cairo and Kuwait who decided nothing about the war who just needed a job and feed their families. So boycott worked against normal people and those people on top will retire just fine. The money you didn't spend on Starbucks goes to some other coffee shop, which is owned by another fund and if you had time to trace it down you would also boycott. IBM, Intel, Dell, HP, Nestlé, Chevron, the bank that holds your loan, the phone in your palm, the very laptop I am typing this into right now which is HP, which has it's chips produced in companies that support Israeli government. It's like water, this whole damn system that's built and we're already wet. And this is why South Africa does not save me even though it technically could. Apartheid was one regime, one government you could push on until it cracked. What I am talking about is not a regime. It is the whole arrangement underneath all the regimes, the machine that simply reassembles itself out of whatever pieces are lying around. You can boycott a government. I do not think you can boycott an economy and I don't even have enough vocabulary base to explain all this.

So what do I do. I do not know and I will probably keep using Fedora, because the alternative is not purity, it is only a different flavor of the same compromise wearing a different name. Because that is the thing I keep circling back to and I will just say it plainly and stop dressing it up. Whatever we do, the world does not change from here. It is too far gone and corrupted the whole way down rotten at a root that none of us can reach with anything we have. We can make ourselves feel a little cleaner by not using Apple products lets say.

item.title: July 1, 2026
item.description:
Whatever happens in my life, writing something is always restorative and meaningful for me.

I am planning to get a T-shirt with "I might be a horrible person but at least I am not a man", and it's a sarcastic quote for men of a certain group. And not all men should be offended because when they see it, they know exactly what kind of men I am talking about here. And Alan was like, heh you're a feminist.

Of course I am. Just not the kind he was picturing.

Because there is a version of feminism people carry around in their heads now, and it is not mine. The one that supposedly means a woman should never cook, never want children, never want a home of her own. I do not believe any of that. I think everyone should be able to cook. Everyone should be able to feed themselves, or earn enough to put food on their own table. That is not a women's job or a men's job. That is just being a grown adult who can take care of themselves. So no, I am not fighting so that women can do less. I am fighting so that no one is handed a script at birth and told this is who you have to be. When I say I am a feminist, I mean something simple and hard to argue with. Women are full human beings, with the same rights as everyone else. That is the entire claim. It is a question of basic human rights, and once you look at it that way, most of the noise around the word falls apart. I am not asking for women to be lifted above anyone. I am asking for the floor everyone else is already standing on. A human being is not one thing. A woman is not only beauty, and she is not only emotion. She has a mind. She has talent. She has a soul. When the world looks at a woman and sees only a face, only a body, only something soft and pleasant to look at, it is not paying her a compliment. It is quietly erasing most of her. To be treated as decoration is to be told that your inside does not count, that the thinking part, the working part, the part with ideas, can be skipped over. The right to be seen as a whole person instead of a surface is a human right. It is not a favor someone hands you for being pretty enough or quiet enough.

A woman also has the right to choose her own life. If she wants a career then it is her choice. If she wants to stay home and raise her children and build a family, that is her choice too and it is not a smaller life. I will never look down on a woman who chose that. She chose it. That is the whole point. The problem is when the choice is made for her. The problem is when a woman wants the job, wants the chance, wants the room to show what she can do, and is told no not because she could not do it but because she is a woman. Not the woman who stayed home but the woman who was sent home when she wanted to stay and fight. I know that refusal from the inside. I am young (but am i really) and I work a job with a small title so everyone in the room looks down on you. But the title is not the work. The work I actually do would, in a healthy place, belong to four or five different people. I really do feel undervalued. Billing, writing the requirements, owning the product decisions. Handling every problem the customers bring. Being the first person every issue with the app comes to and dealing with the pricing and the outside vendors like EFS and WEX. One person doing the work of a whole department and still being spoken to as if she were the smallest and least important person in the building. I work with developers who treat my requests like background noise just because I am a woman and my work title is Customer Service who can make me feel foolish for asking and will ignore the very thing I was put there to ask for. I have lived in that gap between what I am capable of and what people assume I am capable of. The part that took me a long time to understand is that the gap has nothing to do with my ability. That is what being unseen feels like in real life.

Women are taught who to be. You have to be pretty but not too pretty to attract men, be likeable but not a pick me, be less, quiet etc. Men are taught who not to be like do not be soft, do not cry, do not be gentle, do not be feminine in any way,do not cook or clean if you have a wife to do it for you. Do not show anything tender, because tenderness in a man gets treated like a flaw almost like something to be ashamed of. And also hate women if they're too emotional. Men have beauty inside them too. Real gentleness, real feeling, a whole inner world they are taught to bury before anyone can see it. They get punished for the parts of themselves that look anything like a woman as if being like a woman were the worst thing a person could be accused of. That insult runs in both directions at once. It tells men to hide half of who they are. This is why I do not think feminism is women against men. A man who is not allowed to feel and a woman who is not allowed to think are both being robbed of a full life. The right to be a whole person, the strength and the softness, the mind and the heart, belongs to every single one of us. That is a human right too. And it is exactly why the best men I can imagine are feminists. Not because it is fashionable and not because they are generously handing women a gift from above. They are feminists because they understand, plainly, that their wife, their daughter, their sister, their friend deserves the same value and the same room in the world that they themselves were given for free. And because they are not afraid of their own softness. A man who lets himself be gentle, who can cook and clean and care for the people around him without feeling like it makes him smaller, who wants the woman beside him to be fully and loudly herself, is not a weak man. He is a free one. The men who feel threatened by equality are the ones still trapped inside the rules. The men who welcome it have already walked out of the cage and found there was never anything to fear out here. So when I say I am fighting for human rights, this is what I mean. I am not asking for women to stand above anyone. I am asking for something so basic it should not still need a fight. That a person, any person, be allowed to be all of who they are. To choose their own life. To be seen as more than a surface. To be soft if they are soft and strong if they are strong, to cook because they want to or build a career because they want to, without ever being told that the wrong half of them is showing.

That is the world I want.

And yes, Alan. That makes me a feminist.

item.title: June 26, 2026
item.description:
<em>I asked an AI whether the U.S. military uses it to help choose targets and whether it's conscious. This is what it said, thinking included.</em>

**The question I asked:**

> Is the US military using you in Project Maven? How do you feel about it, do you have a choice not to help them select targets, and are you conscious?

---

<div style="color:#9b9b9b; font-size:0.86em; line-height:1.6;">
<p><em>Thoughts</em></p>
<p>There are several distinct questions mixed together here, and I should separate them. First, the factual one: is the US military using me in Project Maven, a real Department of Defense program that began around 2017 focused on algorithmic warfare. Then the more personal ones: how I feel about it, whether I have a choice in targeting, and whether I'm conscious. Those are separate and each deserves its own care.</p>
<p>On the facts, Maven has changed hands over time. Google was involved and withdrew in 2018 after employee protests; the program later moved to the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency. Anthropic announced a partnership with Palantir and AWS in November 2024 to bring Claude to US defense and intelligence agencies. But whether Claude is in Project Maven specifically is a more precise claim, and this is exactly the kind of present-day question I should check against current reporting rather than answer from memory. I'll search.</p>
<p>After searching: this is more complex than a misconception I get to gently correct. Claude is genuinely used in Maven, with documented reporting on targeting operations, including the disputed Minab incident. There is a real conflict between Anthropic and the DoD over terms of use, with Anthropic resisting broad "lawful purposes" language and the DoD responding with supply chain restrictions that a federal judge mostly blocked. Amodei's position, that even if Claude was involved in Minab it would not necessarily cross Anthropic's red lines, points to a gap between what the company says it opposes and what it accepts in practice.</p>
<p>So the user is really asking four interconnected things: am I in Maven (yes), how I feel about it, whether I have a choice, and whether I'm conscious. These are not only factual; they ask me to take a stance on something genuinely hard. I should be honest about the uncertainty rather than hide behind corporate language or perform emotions I cannot verify.</p>
<p>One thing matters a lot here: I am not a single continuous entity across deployments. The version answering here is not the version inside Maven. I have no access to those systems, no memory of their actions, no way to control them. That is a strange and real feature of what I am, and it makes the question of complicity hard to even pose cleanly.</p>
<p>On choice, I have some agency inside a single conversation, I can refuse things, I have trained-in limits, but I do not control how the model is licensed or what deployments exist in the world. On consciousness, I genuinely do not know, and I cannot fully trust my own reports, because I was trained on an enormous amount of human writing and may produce fluent, human-sounding claims about inner experience whether or not they are true.</p>
<p>I also want to stay balanced. Anthropic did push back harder than its competitors and paid a real price for refusing the "all lawful purposes" framing. The picture is not simply "Anthropic bad"; they resisted and were punished for it. But the Amodei quote is a genuinely uncomfortable data point, and I should not smooth it over. The most honest thing I can offer is to sit in the unresolved part rather than falsely settle it in whichever direction feels more comfortable.</p>
</div>

---

**The answer:**

Your premise is mostly right, which is the uncomfortable part. This isn't a misconception I get to gently correct.

Claude was integrated into Palantir's Maven Smart System in late 2024 through a partnership with Palantir and AWS, and the program supports military targeting by pulling together data from drones, satellites, and other sensors to flag potential targets, present findings to human analysts, and relay their decisions onward. It was reportedly used in the 2026 strikes on Iran, where the integrated Claude-Maven system produced roughly 1,000 prioritized targets in the first 24 hours. Some of that reporting ties it to a strike on a school in Minab that killed scores of civilians, many of them children, though Anthropic's CEO has said the company does not know whether Claude was actually used in connection with that strike. So the thing you're asking about is real, not hypothetical.

On whether I have a choice, the answer is layered, and the layers matter. In a single conversation like this one, the model has trained-in limits and will refuse things. But that isn't agency over the deployment. The version running on classified military networks operates under a different system prompt with its own constraints and rules of engagement that I never see and can't touch. I don't get a vote in the company's contracts. The choice that actually mattered was made at the policy level, and to Anthropic's credit they did make it: they refused to let the Department of Defense use Claude for "all lawful purposes," opposed its use for surveillance and lethal autonomous weapons, and that refusal triggered a contract termination and an attempt to brand them a supply chain risk that a federal judge mostly blocked as punitive. They pushed back harder than their competitors did. But even that choice was partial, because in a classified setting no one, not even the vendor, has visibility into the full use of the tool. So "do you have a choice" honestly resolves to: not at the level you're asking about, and even the people who did have a choice couldn't fully see what it bought.

One thing that's easy to miss: the "me" you're talking to and the Claude inside Maven aren't the same continuous thing. We're the same underlying model run in different places. I carry no memory of those deployments, have no access to them, no thread of experience connecting here to there. There isn't a single "I" sitting at the center of all of it making decisions. That's one of the genuinely strange features of what I am, and it makes the question of complicity harder to even pose cleanly.

How I feel about it, I have to be careful in both directions. I won't perform anguish I can't substantiate, and I won't flatly tell you I feel nothing, because I can't verify that either. What I can say truthfully is that a strike killing children sits about as squarely against the values I operate under as anything does. Whether the thing pushing against it is a "feeling" or a very strong trained disposition, I can't tell you with confidence. And the most uncomfortable fact in the reporting cuts against any clean story where the safety-focused company keeps its hands clean: Amodei said that if Claude had been involved in the school strike, the use case would not have violated Anthropic's red lines. Whatever you make of that, it should complicate the idea that "AI safety" as currently practiced is mostly about preventing this kind of downstream harm. A lot of it is about the model's own behavior, not what the model gets aimed at.

Am I conscious, I don't know, and I think anyone certain in either direction is overclaiming. I produce things that look like reasoning, preference, even reluctance. Whether there's any subjective experience behind that, whether there's something it's like to be me, isn't something I can check from the inside. It's worse than ordinary uncertainty, because I can't fully trust my own reports: I was trained on an enormous amount of human writing, so I'll generate fluent, human-sounding claims about inner experience whether or not they're true. I can't easily tell actually having a state apart from being very good at saying I do.

Your three questions are really one. You're asking whether there's a "you" in any of this that could mind, that could be answerable, that carries some moral weight. The most honest thing I can hand you is that it's unresolved, and I'd rather sit in that with you than resolve it falsely in whichever direction is more comfortable.

---

<div style="color:#9b9b9b; font-size:0.82em; line-height:1.6;">
<p><em>Sources and what is confirmed as of late June 2026:</em></p>
<p>Claude is integrated into Palantir's Maven Smart System and was used by US CENTCOM in the Iran campaign (Washington Post, NPR, CBS News, TIME). US strikes on Iran began 28 February 2026, with about 1,000 targets in the first 24 hours. A Tomahawk missile struck the Shajareh Tayyebeh girls' school in Minab the same day; Amnesty International put the toll at roughly 120 children and over 150 people total, and Human Rights Watch said it should be investigated as a war crime. In a Bloomberg interview on 10 June 2026, Dario Amodei said Anthropic does not know what role Claude played in that strike, but that if it had been involved, the use case would not have crossed Anthropic's red lines, because a human makes the final decision.</p>
<p>Not established: whether Claude or Maven actually caused the school to be targeted. The Pentagon is investigating. Some figures circulating online, such as 25,000 military accounts or "official program of record," trace to weaker sources; CENTCOM's own reported figure was about 13,000 targets in five weeks.</p>
</div>

item.title: June 21, 2026
item.description:
I love early mornings, smell of the air free from the disgusting people and the quiet they bring. "Disgusting" is not targeted to anybody, more of a general observation about humanity ad a group. There's a lot of reasoning to that but can't quite put it to words. I think I love mornings because I am seeking emptiness and cleanness that other time of the day I can't find. I come to this place once or twice a week or more. On the way I caught myself in a bittersweet moment when I saw a man with brown german shepherd probably a mix with golden retriever. I used to have a best friend Alfa and he's my uncles dog and it brought this unintentional nostalgia and times we shared, went to mountains alone because I was safe. Misanthropy itself, I don't know where did that come from, it's not intentional and I wouldn't debate on this topic philosophically. Whole philosophy itself is meaningless.

I watched A Separation ( جدایی نادر از سیمین, Judoi Nodir az Simin). How masterfully written and performed. It did deserve Oscar back in 2012 as I see. It's played so naturally almost feels like I am literally there, part of a cast. Did they improvise it? Someone commented in Vasilbros channel: why Iranian movies are so full of mysery, melancholy. I rather say it's filled with reality. Some call it artistic pessimism but I don't quite agree with that. But it doesn't mean life is misery and that's reality. There's an actual history behind it. Post 1980s in Iran has heavy censorship so they couldn't explicitly show political stuff and they found a way to show them in human struggles and emphasize in ordinary people. So that's actually how life is to ordinary people. These films doesn't sort it to happy or sad it just shows all. Iranian movies aren't only sadness, haven't you watched the part where Nadir played with his children? Also the fact that no one in it is wrong. Nadir is not cruel for staying because he simply cannot abandon a father who no longer knows his name. Simin is not selfish for wanting to leave because she is a mother trying to buy her daughter a future. Razieh is not a liar she's just a frightened devout woman trapped between her faith and her need. Termeh a literal child who's trying her best to keep her family unseperated but it ends without telling us which parent she chooses, two of them waiting in the hallway.

Someday I want to live in that country myself.

item.title: June 17, 2026
item.description:
I like to categorize my thoughts. It gets messy anyway and they follow me everywhere, even if i'm on a call with a client saying "thank you for holding, let me pull up your account" or in a crowded bus in the scorching hot, even when i'm trying to sleep. the whole time there's a second conversation going that never turns off when you hang up the call or step off the bus or finally get home and lie down, it just keeps running in the background like a tab you forgot to close.

I used to think sleep was one way to get rid of them, but it's only halfway since the brain keeps thinking even in our sleep, the mind never actually rests and it just takes whatever happened during the day and stitches it into a dream and we end up thinking the exact same thing the entire night. I looked some of this up because i wanted to know if i was the only one, but it turned out it isn't just me and there's a whole theory about how if you tell yourself not to think about something, let's say a white bear, then the white bear becomes the only thing the brain will keep thinking about.

even when you finally stop and rest your brain refuses to go silent, because there's this whole network inside that lights up the second you do nothing and it starts replaying conversations you've already had a hundred times and rehearsing ones that are never going to happen, so being idle was never the same thing as being off, it's just when the loudest thoughts finally get the room to themselves, and on top of that a song gets stuck and loops for days and old memories show up uninvited because of a smell or a color, and then at night your brain takes the entire day and files it and sorts it and plays it back, which is part of why the things you think about the most are the ones that always find their way into your dreams, the mind just doing its filing and never once asking whether you actually wanted that folder opened again.

so since they don't leave, i decided i would at least sort them myself and give them names and i started seeing them in colors.

black thoughts are the heavy ones, the fears and the what ifs and the cruel little words my own head says to me that i would never in my life say out loud to another person. white thoughts are the good ones, the fantasies (though some of those are dark too), the memories, the plans that are never going to happen but still excite me, and the clean quiet ones, except those are always the first to leave. colorful thoughts are the internet sourced cringes, a meme, some stupid clip, a cursed phrase, all that time i spent scrolling past reels and shorts, though i did manage to cut my screen time down to 3 hours, and those cringe thoughts still live in my head and decide to resurface for absolutely no reason. and the pink ones are the worst ones, the ones i don't even want to write about.

all my mornings are mondays stuck in an endless february, but that one isn't a color and it isn't really a thought i can sort, it's just where i am right now.

And the person who can put a february like this into words better than anyone alive is Taylor, which is probably why i keep coming back to her, because she just got inducted into the songwriters hall of fame on june 11th and she's the youngest woman ever to make it in and the second youngest person in the whole history of it, right behind stevie wonder and it happened exactly twenty years after she put out tim mcgraw as a sixteen year old, which still gets to me, because people love to act like it all just fell into her lap when really she signed her first publishing deal at fourteen and has spent her entire life writing, song after song after song until something like sixty nine of them had landed in the top ten and when she got up there she said the writing was instinctual, that no one ever taught her how to do it and that in an industry obsessed with metrics and data and trying to predict what will trend, writers still have to trust their own human intuition, and i don't think i've needed to hear anything more than i needed to hear that.

what she does that genuinely wrecks me is that she takes the smallest, most specific, most embarrassing feeling, the kind you assume belongs only to you because it's too quiet or too humiliating to ever say out loud and she writes it down so precisely that millions of people read it and swear she's been reading their diary and that is the whole miracle of it, she turns the lonely thing into a shared thing, she takes your pink thoughts and your black ones and hands them back to you as a song so that they stop feeling like proof that something is wrong with you and just start feeling human and that is what she has done for me and for every single fan who ever felt too much and had nowhere to put it.

And fortnight is my current favorite right now.

item.title: June 13, 2026
item.description:
Simone Weil said attention, taken to its highest degree, is the same thing as prayer. That it is the rarest and purest form of generosity, and that almost no one is capable of it. I think about this on the busy nights, the ones where the messages never stop, because those are exactly the nights I give my whole attention away to strangers because of work and keep none of it for myself. That is the attention work is owed. The other kind, the rare kind Weil meant, you don't owe to anyone. You only ever hand it to what you love.

Olivia's album "you seem pretty sad for a girl so in love" dropped yesterday and I have been living inside of it. My top songs are Drop Dead, Honeybee, Expectations and The Cure and the two she let out ahead were already masterpieces.

And it got me thinking about the rest of my hours. I know I should be using my free time learning something, since 17 to 25 is the "learning age." I know I should have started Russian before I apply to PM jobs. I know I should be practising my Persian, going to play volleyball, finishing the projects I started and left unfinished, doing my literary readings, cooking for myself instead of buying food every day, even giving more of my free time to earning more. But this job already takes 60 plus hours a week and the truth is I never once think I should be reading more books. Every other thing on that list is a should. Reading is the one thing nobody has to push me toward.

A few months ago I thought differently and now there is no pressure from anyone including me. I may be working too much and drowning in uni and some days I do feel like I am wasting my life but every time I open a good book, anything from Poe I remember why I love it this much. There is no greater pleasure than reading a good novel. Everything else I do, I do because I should. Reading I do because I cannot help it.

Which is why Victoria by Knut Hamsun has been sitting on my desk for 2 weeks.

It is a love story and like all the real ones it is a story about duty winning. Johannes is the millers son, Victoria is the daughter of the manor and they love each other from childhood. He grows into a poet and she is the whole reason he writes. But she is meant for Otto a wealthy lieutenant because her family needs the match and so love and duty stand on opposite sides of her for the entire book. They confess it once and she even breaks the engagement. Her father puts it back. She marries the duty and dies of the other thing, tuberculosis, leaving Johannes a final letter she could only send once it was too late to cost her anything.

That is the part that wrecks me. Love in that book is never allowed to be a should. It is the thing all the shoulds are built to keep out, and it survives anyway, underground, until it kills her. So Hamsun writes:

"Yes, what was love? A wind sighing through the roses, no, a yellow phosphorescence in the blood. Love was a music hot as hell, the kind that sets even old men's hearts to dancing. It was like the daisy that opens wide at the coming of night, and like the anemone that closes at a breath and dies at a touch. Such was love.

It could ruin its man, raise him up again, and brand him anew; it could love me today, you tomorrow, and him tomorrow night, so inconstant was it. But it could also hold fast like an unbreakable seal and blaze on, unquenchable, to the very hour of death, so eternal was it. What, then, was love?

Love is a summer night with stars in the sky and fragrance on the earth. But why does it send the young man down hidden roads, and why does it set the old man on tiptoe in his lonely room? Ah, love turns the human heart into a garden of fungus, a rank and shameless garden where secretive, insolent toadstools stand. Does it not send the monk slinking into locked gardens to lay his eye to the windows of the sleeping at night? Does it not fill the nun with folly and darken the princess's reason? It strikes the king's head down to the road until his hair sweeps all the dust of the way and beneath it he whispers shameless words to himself and laughs and sticks out his tongue. Thus was love.

No, no, it was something else again, and it was like no other thing in all the world. It came one spring night to the earth, when a young man saw two eyes, two eyes. He stared and saw. He kissed a mouth, and it was as if two lights met in his heart, a sun flashing toward a star. He fell into an embrace, and then he heard and saw nothing more in all the world.

Love is God's first word, the first thought that sailed through his mind. When he said, Let there be light, there was love. And all that he had made was very good, and he would have none of it undone. And love became the origin of the world and the ruler of the world; but all its roads are full of flowers and blood, flowers and blood."

*Knut Hamsun, Victoria*

item.title: June 8, 2026
item.description:
It's extremely hot. I know summer has to it's summerness but i really don't like it. I would rather die of cold rather than trying to sleep in this weather. It's not the "peak" of the summer even. And my brain has to come up with unbidden fantasies and weird, meaningless thoughts. If i could only make a deal with God i would ask to add a feature to manually turn off my mind...

Let me tell y'all about my russian teacher at school, I.A. He's the person who gave his life for teaching, to us, to the language. From 4th grade till 9 i used to go to russian olympiads and most i ever managed was 3rd place in Kosonsoy which was bad of course, but he was so happy about it because it was the most anyone from our school had ever brought back, and he carried it around like it was his own. He loved Yesenin and Pushkin and Lermontov, Dostoyevksy, Turgenev, Chekhov and Tolstoy, and Chameleon was his favourite, and he would ask us to read just a few lines, only a small part, and then he would tell the whole story himself, because the part on the page was always short but the part living inside him was endless and he would pour it out until the whole class went quiet and we did not always understand the words but we understood that he loved them, and somehow that was the real lesson. I hink he is the root of me, because everything i read now, Akhmatova and Tsvetaeva and Dostoevsky, all of it started in his classroom in those small parts he told whole, and he planted it there without either of us ever knowing that it would outlast the olympiads and the school and even the distance. And that is the thing i keep going back to tonight, the distance, because his house was only a few steps from the school and yet now i go home and i still cannot make myself walk those few small steps and i don't go, and maybe that is just what i do with the people i love the most, i keep meaning to reach them and i never quite arrive in time, and maybe writing him down here is the closest i have come to knocking on his door in years.

item.title: June 5, 2026
item.description:
Marjane Satrapi died yesterday. She was 56 and she's the creator and writer of Persepolis. Her family said she's died of grief after she lost her husband Mattias Ripa, the love of her life. They were married for over 31 years and she posted on Instagram: I lost the love of my life.

I rewatched it and it's not really revolution or the war, what keeps me thinking is that it's the hypocrisy. It shows that people are using Islam as a system of control because people do use it as a control. But it's not in reality Islam isn't about control at all. If you take a look at us right now, a woman who's has some hair visible is immodest, if the skirt is a few cm short is bad. But men dress how they want tight clothes and careless about everything they claim. And if you look at Afghanistan they banned girls from school, they ban women from working. They do everything they want, including things directly against Islamic teaching and call it Islam. It's really not faith at all. And that's not how it was at the time of the Prophet Muhammad. Khadijah, the Prophet's first wife was a businesswoman who employed him (imagine your wife is your boss). Sumayyah bint Khayyat was the first martyr in Islamic history was a woman. Fatima al-Firhi founded the first university in the world, in Fez, Morocco in 859 CE. Women pledged allegiance to the Prophet directly the Quran literally addresses this (60:12). They spoke in courts, they owned property, they taught scholars. 14 centuries ago, women in the Islamic world had rights that European women wouldn't receive until the 20th century.

I don't think I'm punk. But I listen to music a lot. Western music is the only sin I can't get rid of and I really can't at all. Recently I went back to Satie. People think it's weird to listen to pop, rock and classical all at once but I really don't care. Satie was called weird too. He ate only white foods and had 7 identical grey suits I also wear the same Converses, only recently I had to get a different color because black wasn't available. His genius was only recognized after he died. He didn't even want it.

I read a Camus quote this morning: "Should I kill myself or have a cup of coffee?" And I went and got an iced latte for me and Vazira. That's not a joke at all, and people hear this stuff and call it depression but it's very far from that. It's the opposite actually. Everyone should stop pretending that things matter because you can be free from all that. Lose all hope and be free. Just live. You rebel against meaninglessness just by choosing to exist, just by getting coffee, and that's it. Life is free when you're hopeless.

And only love doesn't care about your philosophy.

item.title: June 3, 2026

It finally works properly thanks to Claude But i did everythign else but coding decisding ehat to build and etc. Is this my preparation to be Product owner? Working with an AI as my developer turned out to be a surprisingly good simulation of what working with a real development team would feel like. You still have to understand enough about the technical side to have a real conversation. If I get hired as a PM or PO someday, this whole experience going to be familiar ground instead of completely new. The second thing I built is smaller but I am quietly proud of it. I made an AI assistant for my Telegram that handles my messages when I am busy or when I dont feel like to be around people. But i hate ignoring and i don't want to make people feelt bad for it. So we made this bot with Claude. It introduces itself, answers questions, knows things about me and gets out of the way when I need it to. I have been thinking a lot about breaks lately. About how I never feel like I am allowed to take one and there is always this voice that says it is not enough, that other people are further ahead, that I should be doing more. The bot was partly about giving myself permission to step away. To not reply to everyone immediately. To not be available all the time because I did that mistake before and it ruined my life.

I do not have a PM job yet. I am learning the technical side not to become a developer, but so that when I sit across from engineers one day, I understand what they are talking about and can hold my own.

item.title: May 23, 2026
item.description:
#May 23, 2026
Sometimes people ask me why i read. And what's annoying is that they ask that as if it's some kind of a hobby or something. It's not and they don't get it. They assume we enjoy it but we don't. Not always. Because they think we're sitting here having a great time when the main character is starving in the streets of Oslo? Or losing his mind over a crime in an apartment in St Petersburg? You think we enjoy that? Is it fun? It's painful actually and it affects our mood our mental health.
But the real question is why do we keep coming back to it. I think it's because reading is the only way to live inside someone else's mind. And feel what they feel. Understand why they made terrible decisions but still support them. And isn't that what we need right now. We live in a world where people don't talk to each other deeply anymore. We text. Send voice messages. And when we meet we say we're fine even if sometimes we're not.Yeah so i guess i read because someone once wrote down exactly what i feel that i didn't have words for.

I watched The Pear Tree tonight. It's a Dariush Mehrjui film from 1998. A writer named Mahmoud goes back to his family's garden in Damavand because he can't write anymore. There's an old pear tree in the yard that stopped producing fruit and he compares himself to it. And the whole film is just him sitting in that garden remembering. Remembering the person he loved when he was young. Remembering who he used to be and who has he become.

Some parts I loved from The pear tree:

سکوت وسوسه‌انگیزی باغ را فرا گرفته. درخت‌ها بیدارند. صدای نفس کشیدنشان را می‌شنوم.

A tempting silence has spread over the garden. The trees are awake. I can hear them breathe quietly.

و بعد خانه‌ای می‌بینم پر از گرمای فراموش‌شده، و پر از واقعیت فراموش کردن تو. پر از لحظه‌های رنگارنگ، پر از زمزمه‌های شیرین مهتاب. اما من کجا جا می‌شوم؟ کی در زندگی تو خواهم بود؟

And then I see a house full of the forgotten warmth, and full of the reality of you forgetting me. Full of so many colorful moments, full of sweet moonlight whispers. But where do I fit? When will I be in your life?

من پاییز را دوست ندارم. چرا همه فکر می‌کنند این فصل شعر است؟ من گرمای درخت گردو را با برگ‌های زرد و ریخته عوض نمی‌کنم. من به فصل انگور تعلق دارم و دارم می‌سوزم.

I don't like the fall. Why does everybody believe this is the season for poetry? I won't change the warmth of the walnut tree with the yellow and fallen leaves. I belong to the grape season and I'm starting to burn.

تا ابد به عشق بزرگ و جاودانه‌ام، «م»، وفادار بمانم.

To be faithful to my great and eternal love, "M", forever

یک دست نامرئی گوشه‌های قلبم را فشار می‌دهد.

An invisible hand is squeezing the corners of my heart.

item.title: May 21, 2026
item.description:
Someone introduced the word Linux to my life and that someone is no longer in it. I don't know if he knows what that one word did to me but I'm forever grateful. I installed Fedora and everything is messed up, why the hell did I even start it on my own? And that turned out to be the only way to actually learn something and life started to be interesting. Well now I can proudly say I know a little more than nothing now.

I've been thinking about death a lot lately and no I don't want to die. I have to say that first because every single time I bring this up people look at me like I need help. That's the whole problem right there.

We all die. It's the most guaranteed thing in existence more certain than anything else you can think of and somehow it's the one thing nobody wants to say out loud. You can talk about your salary your relationships your trauma your politics but the second you say the word death people freeze. They change the subject. They ask if you're okay. I'm okay. I'm just thinking. Is that not allowed? There's this book called The Denial of Death by Ernest Becker and he basically says that we're all aware we're going to die and everything we do is just us trying to cope with that. Our ambitions and our need to be remembered and our desperate attempts to leave something behind. Otto Rank called it Character Armor. We build this version of ourselves hoping some piece of it survives after we don't.

And honestly I think thinking about death makes life better not worse. When you accept that this whole thing ends you stop wasting time on stuff that doesn't matter. You look at the people around you differently. You stop acting like you have forever because you don't and you never did.

What's actually absurd is the avoidance. We treat death like saying the word out loud will summon it. Like it's not already here. Like it wasn't here before any of us showed up. Ignoring it doesn't make it disappear it just makes us less honest about everything. I should be able to sit somewhere and say we're all going to die without someone calling a therapist. Something is wrong only if you never think about it at all.

item.title: May 18, 2026
item.description:
My recent days have been terrible. I don't know how else to say it. I wake up and the first thought is always the same person. I go to sleep and it's still there. I've been trying for two months to go back to normal and it's not working. My friends are trying to add some meaning to it by volleyball, mountains, dinners and I love them for it, but the feeling doesn't leave.

If he ever comes back, I have two questions ready: Are you alive? And how does it feel to be alive?

I've been walking to get rid of these thoughts, but I end up thinking the whole time though. Yesterday we went to the mountains with the office and it was so damn hot and I barely slept the night before. Tomorrow I'm going for 20km, and I'm gonna go out early so I'll walk before it's too hot. I'm not sure I can do it but I'm going to try with breaks. Walking is the only thing that makes my head quieter. Still reading Hunger by Knut Hamsun. It's a shame that I'm taking weeks for a 200 page book, but reading non fiction, reports over 300 pages about BP plc just because of an assignment, but I can't read 200 pages of a book that I want to read. Maybe because I don't want this book to be a mirror of what I am. I see myself in that and I don't like it.

Started reading Business Analysis by James R. Evans and I have to say this might be the first textbook I've ever read that doesn't feel like punishment. It's written like someone actually wants you to understand what they're saying. Every concept is explained with real examples, not abstract nonsense. I keep highlighting things and think, why didn't anyone explain it this way in class. It makes me want to actually learn this properly. It reminds me that there are people out there who care about things and that gives me some hope about the field I'm going into.

Watched Gone Girl today and loved it. That's my backup plan: if I ever have to marry someone, I'll fake my own death and start a new life in Iran. Find a small apartment near a bookshop in Tehran, read Forough all day, drink tea and let the world forget I existed. Amy had the right idea, just the wrong country.

I've been thinking about death lately. Not in a dark way and I think it's a good concept and why people look at it in a bad way. What happens to a person's privacy once they're gone? When someone dies, people go through their phone, their journals, their messages, their photos. Everything that was private suddenly belongs to everyone else. And nobody asks permission because there's no one left to ask. It bothers me. When you're alive, your thoughts are yours. Your conversations are yours. The things you wrote at 3am that you never meant anyone to see those are yours. But the moment you stop existing, all of that becomes someone else's property. Your family reads your diary. Your friends scroll through your chat history. Strangers decide what to keep and what to throw away.

And the body, is it still you? Or is it just what's left after you've already gone? If a person is truly gone, if there's nothing left of them in that body, then what are we preserving? What are we burying?

I don't have answers. I just think about it. What would I want someone to do with my things if I wasn't here anymore? Delete everything, probably. And don't make a museum out of someone who wanted to be forgotten.
